Spanish Constitution of 1876: Catholicism as state religion; no dividing line between Church and State; civil authorities exercised religious functions; friars exercised civil powers
American alteration: Treaty of Paris (December 10, 1898) guaranteed religious freedom in the Philippines

Non-establishment clause: purposes are (1) encourage voluntarism; (2) insulate the political process from interfaith dissension; government must be neutral on religious matters

Free exercise clause: freedom of belief is 'as limitless as one's imagination and thought'; but exercise of religious belief can be regulated; the Philippine SC tries to carve out exceptions to accommodate religious exercise when justified

one_paragraph_summary: Delivered January 29, 2008 at Bulacan State University -- where CJP holds an honorary Doctor of Laws and considers himself a BSU alumnus ('itinuring ko na po ang aking sarili na isa na ring alumnus ng BSU') -- on the occasion of the Malolos Constitution celebration, this bilingual address (Filipino opening and close; English main body) argues that the Malolos Constitution deserves celebration not only as a symbol of independence but because it proves that the Philippines was already a constitutional democracy over 100 years ago. The speech then tackles whether priests commenting on corruption/EJKs and officials attending prayer rallies violate church-state separation. The historical context: the 1876 Spanish Constitution made Catholicism the state religion (friars exercised civil powers; civil authorities performed religious functions); the 1898 Treaty of Paris guaranteed religious freedom; on January 22, 1899, the Malolos Constitution's Article 5 declared 'The State recognizes the freedom and equality of all religions, as well as the separation of the Church and the State.' CJP analyzes the non-establishment clause (two purposes: encourage voluntarism; insulate political process from interfaith dissension; government must be neutral on religion) and the free exercise clause (freedom of belief is limitless; exercise can be regulated; Philippine SC carves out exceptions to accommodate religious exercise). His conclusion: the Philippines has evolved a 'uniquely Filipino' concept of church-state separation over 100 years -- different from the strict US atheistic model; 'the Philippines is theist, not atheist, not even agnostic. In fact, it is monotheist; it worships one God. That is why, its concepts and interpretations of the separation of the Church and the State... have been evolved over the last one hundred years in a uniquely Filipino manner, as the Malolos Constitution itself is uniquely Filipino.' Evidence: Cabinet sessions, Congressional sessions, and court hearings all open with invocations.
